summary.text: At \(n=473165\), \(a(n)=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779\), and the interior number \(k=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783=a(n)+4\) is Sierpiński.  A covering of the 48 exponent residues by primes \(3,5,7,17,97,257,673\), each satisfying \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p\), shows that every \(k2^m+1\) has a proper divisor, so \(k\) lies strictly between the claimed consecutive pair.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9454129+11184810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(k>1\) such that, for every positive integer \(m\), the number
\[
k2^m+1
\]
is composite (equivalently, is not prime).

We disprove the assertion by considering the index
\[
n_0=473165
\]
and the integer
\[
K=5292270077783.
\]
We will first prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number, using a covering of all possible exponents modulo \(48\).

For each residue \(r\in\{0,1,\ldots,47\}\), assign a divisor according to the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{condition on }r & p & K\pmod p & \text{basic exponent congruence}\pmod p\\ \hline
r\equiv0\pmod 2 & 3 & 2 & 2^0\equiv1\\
r\equiv3\pmod 4 & 5 & 3 & 2^3\equiv3\\
r\in\{1,13,25,37\} & 7 & 3 & 2^1\equiv2\\
r\in\{9,17,33,41\} & 17 & 8 & 2^1\equiv2\\
r\in\{5,21\} & 257 & 8 & 2^5\equiv32\\
r=29 & 97 & 94 & 2^{29}\equiv65\\
r=45 & 673 & 665 & 2^{45}\equiv589
\end{array}
\]

These rows cover every residue from \(0\) through \(47\). Indeed, the first row covers all even residues. Of the odd residues, the second row covers those congruent to \(3\) modulo \(4\). The remaining residues, those congruent to \(1\) modulo \(4\), are
\[
1,5,9,13,17,21,25,29,33,37,41,45,
\]
and these are exactly distributed among the last five rows as displayed.

We now justify the modular arithmetic in the table and show its significance. First, direct division of \(K\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p&K\pmod p\\ \hline
3&2\\
5&3\\
7&3\\
17&8\\
257&8\\
97&94\\
673&665.
\end{array}
\]
For example, the corresponding quotient-remainder decompositions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=3(1764090025927)+2,\\
K&=5(1058454015556)+3,\\
K&=7(756038582540)+3,\\
K&=17(311310004575)+8,\\
K&=257(20592490575)+8,\\
K&=97(54559485337)+94,\\
K&=673(7863699966)+665.
\end{aligned}
\]

Moreover, in every row we have
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
For \(p=3,5,7,17,257\), this follows respectively from the elementary periods
\[
2^2\equiv1\pmod3,
\quad 2^4\equiv1\pmod5,
\quad 2^3\equiv1\pmod7,
\quad 2^8\equiv1\pmod{17},
\quad 2^{16}\equiv1\pmod{257},
\]
since \(2,4,3,8,16\) all divide \(48\). The last two congruences can be seen directly by repeated squaring. Modulo \(97\),
\[
2^8\equiv62,
\qquad 2^{16}\equiv61,
\qquad 2^{24}\equiv61\cdot62\equiv96\equiv-1,
\]
so \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod{97}\). Also,
\[
2^{29}=2^{24}2^4 2\equiv(-1)\cdot16\cdot2\equiv65\pmod{97}.
\]
Modulo \(673\),
\[
2^8=256,
\qquad 2^{16}\equiv255,
\qquad 2^{24}\equiv255\cdot256\equiv-1,
\]
because \(255\cdot256=65280=97\cdot673-1\). Hence again \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod{673}\), and
\[
2^{45}=2^{24}2^{16}2^4 2
 \equiv(-1)\cdot255\cdot16\cdot2
 \equiv589\pmod{673}.
\]
For later use, the other basic period calculations also show that the displayed exponent congruence in each row remains valid throughout that row. More explicitly:

* If \(r\) is even, then \(2^r\equiv1\pmod3\).
* If \(r\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(2^r\equiv2^3\equiv3\pmod5\).
* The exponents \(1,13,25,37\) are all congruent to \(1\) modulo \(3\), so \(2^r\equiv2\pmod7\).
* The exponents \(9,17,33,41\) are all congruent to \(1\) modulo \(8\), so \(2^r\equiv2\pmod{17}\).
* The exponents \(5,21\) are congruent to \(5\) modulo \(16\), so \(2^r\equiv2^5=32\pmod{257}\).

It follows in every case that
\[
K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Indeed, row by row, the relevant products are
\[
2\cdot1+1=3,
\quad 3\cdot3+1=10,
\quad 3\cdot2+1=7,
\quad 8\cdot2+1=17,
\quad 8\cdot32+1=257.
\]
For the final two rows,
\[
94\cdot65+1=6111=63\cdot97,
\]
and
\[
665\cdot589+1=391686=582\cdot673.
\]
Thus the table proves the following finite covering statement: for every \(r\) with \(0\le r<48\), at least one number
\[
p\in\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}
\]
satisfies both
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p
\quad\text{and}\quad
K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]

Now let \(m\) be any positive integer. By Euclidean division, write
\[
m=48q+r,
\qquad 0\le r<48.
\]
Choose \(p\) from the covering table for this residue \(r\). Since \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p\),
\[
2^m=2^{48q+r}=2^r(2^{48})^q\equiv2^r\pmod p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
K2^m+1\equiv K2^r+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(p\) divides \(K2^m+1\).

This divisor is proper. Every possible \(p\) satisfies
\[
2\le p\le673,
\]
whereas, because \(m>0\),
\[
K2^m+1\ge2K+1>673.
\]
Therefore \(K2^m+1\) has a divisor strictly between \(1\) and itself and hence is composite. Since this holds for every positive \(m\), and since \(K=5292270077783\) is odd and greater than \(1\), \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

It remains to locate \(K\) between the two terms claimed to be consecutive. A direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(473165)
&=9454129+11184810\cdot473165\\
&=5292270077779.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
a(473165)=5292270077779<K=5292270077783,
\]
the difference being \(4\). On the other hand,
\[
a(473165)+28=5292270077807>K,
\]
the difference being \(24\). Hence
\[
a(473165)<K<a(473165)+28.
\]

We have therefore exhibited a Sierpiński number \(K\) strictly between \(a(473165)\) and \(a(473165)+28\). Those two integers cannot be consecutive Sierpiński numbers. Consequently the assertion that \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\) are consecutive Sierpiński numbers for every \(n\ge0\) is false.
